title: When Economic Statecraft Stops Biting
hook: Tariffs and export controls are the two big levers of economic security policy. Both have a habit of losing force the longer they stay pulled.
key_points: Economic statecraft means using trade and technology access — not troops — to change another state's behavior.
Tariffs tax imports to raise a rival's costs; export controls deny it specific goods, above all advanced technology.
NPR reports that both tools, central to the Trump administration's economic security strategy, are currently hitting snags.
Leverage erodes predictably: trade reroutes through third countries, targets build substitutes, and partners retaliate.
Costs also land at home, on importers and consumers, which makes sustaining the pressure politically expensive.
content_html: Governments that want to change another state's behavior without going to war reach for economic tools. Two dominate the current toolkit: tariffs, which tax imports to raise a rival's costs and shrink its market access, and export controls, which cut a country off from specific goods — most consequentially advanced chips and the equipment used to make them. NPR's Emily Feng reports that both, the Trump administration's main economic security instruments, are running into trouble at the same time.
extra_html: That is a familiar pattern rather than a surprise, and the reason is structural. Economic restrictions are strongest the moment they land and weaker every month afterward, because they hand everyone affected an incentive to route around them: goods travel through third countries, buyers find alternative suppliers, and the targeted state pours money into building its own substitute for whatever it was denied. Meanwhile the pressure runs in both directions. Tariffs are paid in the first instance by domestic importers and passed toward consumers, export controls cost domestic firms their customers, and trading partners answer with measures of their own. The result is a policy that has to be maintained against mounting domestic complaint precisely as its bite fades — which is why economic statecraft so often produces long stalemates rather than quick concessions. (U.S. examples; the same mechanics show up wherever states use market access as leverage.)

related.title: Tariffs Aimed at Behavior, Not Just Trade
related.hook: A new round of U.S. tariffs was justified not as shielding domestic industry but as punishing countries for weak enforcement of forced-labor bans — trade policy used as a lever on someone else's laws.

related.title: Why Tariff Fights Escalate
related.hook: The U.S. put 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods; Canada said within hours it would hit back. That reflex — retaliate, don't absorb — is what turns a tariff into a trade war.

related.title: Sanctions: The Weapon States Reach For Before They Reach For Weapons
related.hook: Cutting a country off from money and markets sits between a strongly-worded letter and a war — which is exactly why governments use it so often, and why it so often disappoints.

related.title: Trade & Protectionism
related.hook: Should a country trade freely with the world or shield its own industries? This single question has driven economic politics for centuries — and still does.

flashcards.prompt: What is economic statecraft, and what are its two headline tools here?
flashcards.back_html: Using economic access rather than force to change another state's behavior — here, tariffs (taxing imports) and export controls (denying a country specific goods, especially advanced technology).

flashcards.prompt: Why does the leverage from tariffs and export controls tend to erode over time?

choices.text: Trade reroutes through third countries, targets develop substitutes, and partners retaliate
International law caps how long any tariff may remain in force
Tariffs automatically expire unless a treaty renews them each year

flashcards.explanation_html: Restrictions create incentives to work around them. Given time, supply chains reroute, substitutes appear, and counter-measures arrive.

flashcards.prompt: Why is sustaining this kind of pressure politically costly for the government applying it?

choices.text: A share of the cost lands at home, on domestic importers and consumers
The targeted country must be compensated for lost trade
Legislatures are required to hold a public vote every quarter

flashcards.explanation_html: Tariffs raise prices for domestic buyers and export controls cut off sales for domestic firms, so pressure abroad creates complaints at home.
